central_question: From 21 October 2026 through the first round of the French presidential election scheduled for 18 April 2027, how will France's budgetary crisis, minority-government instability and the October 2026 riots resolve across fiscal, public-order, government-survival, electoral and market outcomes?

situation_brief.current_situation: Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's minority government presented the PLF 2027 on 1 October 2026 into a hung National Assembly where every budget since 2024 has passed only via Article 49.3; the solemn first-part vote was postponed from 20 October with more than 2,800 amendments pending, and France has just experienced its worst unrest in years over 17-19 October 2026, with roughly 3,000 shops looted, ~2,400 arrests and targeted curfews in several cities.
situation_brief.context: Three prime ministers (Attal, Bayrou, Lecornu) have cycled through office in 2024-26. The revised 2026 deficit forecast is 5.4% of GDP (government), with the Commission at 5.1% (2026) and 5.7% (2027, unchanged policies); debt stands at 119.0% of GDP (end-Q2 2026); France remains under the EU Excessive Deficit Procedure. The 10-year OAT-Bund spread hit a one-year high of 150.8 bps on 20 October 2026, with French yields above Italy's and Greece's. Le Pen leads first-round polls at 32.5-38%.
situation_brief.dynamics: The budget path runs through a probable floor rejection, a possible 49.3 engagement (whole-budget vote reported for 17 November), and censure risk hinging on a ~20-vote gap supplied by PS abstention (left's high-water mark: 269 of 289 votes). Riot recurrence before April 2027 is the swing variable: three of four prior severe episodes were followed by another within five years, at a shortening interval (~3 years from 2023 to 2026). Legally, the election dates (18 April / 2 May 2027) cannot be moved by emergency regimes; the 2017 election was held under a state of emergency.
fault_lines: Minority government vs Assembly arithmetic: 289-vote censure threshold vs left's 269-vote peak
Austerity and EDP consolidation vs weak growth (0.841% in 2025) and rising interest charges (€91.2bn in 2027)
Order-and-security salience from the riots vs cost-of-living grievances on the left
RN's preference to wait for April 2027 rather than govern via censure
Centre fragmentation: Philippe vs Attal vs Macron-affiliated bloc
State-backed riot-insurance mechanism created by the 2026 budget law not yet operational
catalysts: Moody's review of France's Aa3/Negative rating, 23 October 2026
Any 49.3 engagement on the PLF 2027 and ensuing censure motion
France Assureurs' first riot loss estimate and any catastrophe declaration
Renewed or fading protest weekends; curfew extensions or a 1955 state-of-emergency declaration
INSEE's first full-year 2026 deficit estimate, spring 2027
First round of the presidential election, 18 April 2027

scenarios.name: Muddle-through austerity
scenarios.narrative: The minority government passes the 2027 budget via 49.3, survives censure narrowly, de-escalation follows the riots, the deficit lands near 5-5.5 percent and the election proceeds on schedule with RN qualifying first.

scenarios.name: Escalation and paralysis
scenarios.narrative: Recurring riots force emergency measures, censeure or resignation produces a caretaker technocratic cabinet, the budget slips past 31 December 2026, spreads widen sharply and security salience boosts RN further.

scenarios.name: Censure and left surge
scenarios.narrative: A censure motion over the budget topples the government, new instability shifts the race toward the left-wing coalition, fiscal consolidation stalls and the deficit exceeds 5.5 percent.

scenarios.name: Stabilisation rebound
scenarios.narrative: Markets and polling recover as unrest fades and a cross-party budget deal is enacted without 49.3, tightening the spread and lifting Macron-affiliated and centre-right prospects into the runoff.

drivers.direction: raises probability of enactment before 31 December 2026 and of Muddle-through austerity
drivers.why_it_matters: minority governments since 2024 have passed budgets only via 49.3, and censure after a 49.3 voids the bill [S5]

drivers.variable: Censure tally margin supplied by the Socialist Party
drivers.direction: a PS shift toward censure raises government-fall probability
drivers.why_it_matters: the left's high-water mark of 269 votes fell 20 short of the 289 threshold, with the PS abstaining [S40][S41][S28]

drivers.variable: Riot recurrence before the first round
drivers.direction: raises Escalation and paralysis probability and RN vote share via security salience
drivers.why_it_matters: 3 of 4 severe episodes recurred within five years at a shrinking ~3-year interval, and about 3,000 looted shops already exceed 2023's ~2,500 [S48][S14]

drivers.direction: losses above the 2023 EUR 730-793 million benchmark push toward escalation
drivers.why_it_matters: Morningstar caps October 2026 losses below EUR 1.2 billion only assuming no further widespread riots, and early tallies revise upward [S48][S14]

drivers.variable: 2026 deficit slippage versus the 5.5 percent threshold
drivers.direction: exceedance requires ~0.1 pp of fresh slippage beyond the government's 5.4 percent
drivers.why_it_matters: all published baselines (5.4% government, 5.1% Commission, -5.352% IMF) sit below 5.5%, with no cyclical cushion from 0.841% growth in 2025 [S4][S7][S8][S9]

drivers.direction: sustained widening above the high-150s signals escalation; retreat toward the 77.8 bps average signals stabilisation
drivers.why_it_matters: the spread hit a one-year high of 150.8 bps on 20 Oct 2026 against an all-time high of 225.1 bps on 17 Nov 2011 [S12]

drivers.variable: Sovereign rating actions and mechanical bank downgrades
drivers.direction: a Moody's cut from Aa3 pressures French banks downward and widens spreads
drivers.why_it_matters: seven French banks were cut to A1 from Aa3 on 17 Dec 2024 purely via reduced government-support uplift after the sovereign cut [S65][S66]

drivers.variable: Centrist fragmentation (Philippe vs Attal vote split)
drivers.direction: fragmentation lowers the chance of a Macron-affiliated or centre-right runoff qualification
drivers.why_it_matters: Philippe fell to 12% from 15% while Attal polls 7-11%, splitting the anti-RN centre [S17][S16]
